member.name: M:RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.ParseWhereClause``1(RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.RDFQueryParserContext,``0)

summary.para: Parses the WHERE clause of a SELECT query and attaches the resulting algebra members to

SPARQL grammar: WhereClause ::= 'WHERE'? GroupGraphPattern. The WHERE keyword is optional: a query that opens its body with a bare { is perfectly valid, so this method first tries to consume WHERE and then unconditionally expects the opening brace.

The body of the group graph pattern is parsed by , which implements the full graph-pattern algebra (OPTIONAL, UNION, MINUS) and returns a flat list of already-combined algebra nodes. Each node is then attached to the query via so that the engine's evaluator can walk them directly.

member.exception: When the braces are unbalanced or a member is malformed.

member.name: M:RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.ParseGroupGraphPatternSub(RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.RDFQueryParserContext)

summary.para: Parses the content of a GroupGraphPattern body (i.e. everything between its braces) and returns the ordered, flat list of algebra members it produces. The caller is responsible for consuming the surrounding { and } characters — this method only sees what is inside.

SPARQL grammar:
GroupGraphPatternSub ::= TriplesBlock? ( GraphPatternNotTriples '.'? TriplesBlock? )*
GraphPatternNotTriples ::= GroupOrUnionGraphPattern | OptionalGraphPattern | MinusGraphPattern | GraphGraphPattern | ServiceGraphPattern | Filter | Bind | InlineData

Algebra accumulation rules. The grouping/binding of well-formed input is strictly SPARQL-compliant (e.g. MINUS binds the whole accumulated left side); on top of that the parser applies two RATIFIED leniencies for malformed input — a stray UNION and a leading MINUS are recovered from rather than rejected (see the corresponding items below):
BGP (bare triples) — a triple run is read by into a new and appended to the accumulator.
GroupOrUnionGraphPattern { … } — delegated to ; a UNION chain inside the braces is folded into a single left-associative tree node before being appended.
OPTIONAL — the following GroupGraphPattern operand is parsed, its IsOptional flag is set to true, and it is appended to the accumulator as an independently optional element.
MINUS — per the SPARQL spec, MINUS binds the ENTIRE left side accumulated so far (not just the immediately preceding element). The current accumulator is therefore collapsed to a single algebra unit — wrapping in a SELECT * subquery when it contains more than one joined member — and an (Minus, collapsedLeft, right) tree node replaces the entire accumulator. A leading MINUS with an empty accumulator is treated resiliently: the right operand is kept as a plain non-MINUS element.
Stray UNION — UNION appearing at this level (rather than inside a GroupOrUnionGraphPattern) has no valid left operand. It is silently discarded and parsing continues, so that the parser is lenient toward malformed queries.
GRAPH — delegated to : the following group is parsed with the parsed graph specifier (a fixed or an ) fixed as the per-pattern context of every triple it contains, then appended like any other element.
Other graph-pattern keywords (FILTER, BIND, VALUES, SELECT sub-select, SERVICE) — each is delegated to its dedicated parser and appended as the appropriate member; any keyword whose phase has not landed yet still raises an explicit "not supported yet" parse error.

member.returns: A list of zero or more instances (pattern groups, subqueries, and operator tree nodes) in left-to-right order, ready to be attached to the enclosing query.
member.exception: On unbalanced braces, malformed triples, or unsupported keywords.

member.name: M:RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.AppendBasicGraphPatternMember(RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.RDFQueryParserContext,System.Collections.Generic.List{RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryMember},System.Collections.Generic.List{RDFSharp.Query.RDFFilter})
member.summary: Parses a basic graph pattern run and appends it to the current group body

member.name: M:RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.ParseGroupGraphPattern(RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.RDFQueryParserContext)

summary.para: Parses a single GroupGraphPattern — a { … } delimited block — and collapses its contents to a single algebra member. The surrounding braces are consumed by this method; the body is parsed by .

When the body expands to more than one joined member, they are automatically wrapped in a SELECT * subquery via so that the caller always receives a single algebra unit. This is necessary for correct MINUS semantics (the whole compound group must act as one operand) and for correct UNION semantics (each branch must be a single member).

member.returns: A single representing the entire group: a bare for a single-element body, an wrapping multiple joined members, or an empty for an empty body.
member.exception: When the opening brace is missing or the body is malformed.

member.name: M:RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.ParseGroupOrUnionGraphPattern(RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.RDFQueryParserContext)

summary.para: Parses a GroupOrUnionGraphPattern — the construct that starts with a { and may be followed by one or more UNION { … } continuations — and returns a single algebra member.
SPARQL grammar: GroupOrUnionGraphPattern ::= GroupGraphPattern ( 'UNION' GroupGraphPattern )*.

A bare group with no UNION continuation is returned as-is from . A chain of two or more groups connected by UNION is folded left-to-right into a binary (Union, left, right) tree, matching the spec's left-associative union semantics:
A UNION B UNION C → Union( Union(A, B), C )

WHITESPACE PROTOCOL: never skips leading whitespace (callers must ensure the reader is on a significant character before calling it). After each call the reader lands on the character immediately following the closing }, which is typically a space. Therefore MUST be called before every UNION peek — once before the while loop and once at the end of each iteration — to keep the reader positioned correctly for the keyword scan.

member.returns: A single representing either the bare group or the root of the left-associative UNION algebra tree.
member.exception: When any operand group is malformed.

member.name: M:RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.ParseGraphGraphPattern(RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.RDFQueryParserContext)

summary.para: Parses a GraphGraphPattern — the GRAPH keyword (already consumed by the caller), followed by a graph specifier and a GroupGraphPattern — and returns the single algebra member the braces collapse to. Every triple pattern produced inside the braces is decorated with the parsed graph context.
SPARQL grammar: GraphGraphPattern ::= 'GRAPH' VarOrIri GroupGraphPattern.

MODEL MAPPING. RDFSharp has no explicit Graph(var, P) algebra node: GRAPH is represented by fixing the context on each individual (the four-argument constructor). This is faithful to the spec because the SHARED context — same object, or same — is the join key: when the specifier is a variable, the engine binds it per-quadruple for every contextualised pattern and joins on it, forcing all those patterns into the same named graph (exactly ∪_g eval(P against graph g)); when it is a fixed IRI, the engine filters every contextualised pattern to that one graph. The runtime target of GRAPH is therefore an (the RDF dataset); against a single the engine ignores the context, which is the correct SPARQL behaviour (a lone graph is just the default graph).

CONTEXT DISCIPLINE (save → set → recurse → restore). The graph context is pushed onto the shared slot for the duration of the inner call and then popped back. This single mutable slot, bracketed per dispatch, yields SPARQL §18.4 innermost shadowing for free: a nested GRAPH overrides the slot for its own sub-scope and restores the enclosing context on exit, so each triple pattern is bound to the graph of the GRAPH clause that most tightly encloses it (e.g. in GRAPH ?g { ?s ?p ?o GRAPH ?h { ?a ?b ?c } } the ?s ?p ?o pattern is contextualised by ?g while ?a ?b ?c is contextualised by ?h).

EMPTY GRAPH REJECTION. An empty group (GRAPH ?g {} or GRAPH <iri> {}) is rejected with an . The per-pattern model cannot represent it: a SPARQL empty group is the join identity (a single empty solution), so GRAPH ?g {} would ENUMERATE the named graphs (one solution per graph, with ?g bound to each graph IRI) — but with no pattern to carry the context there is nothing to bind ?g to. Rather than silently produce a wrong result we reject. Detection is exact via the WasUsed flag, which is true iff at least one pattern was actually built under THIS clause's context (a nested GRAPH does not satisfy its parent's check, because the discipline brackets the flag too).

member.returns: The single algebra member the GRAPH's group graph pattern collapses to.
member.exception: When the graph specifier is malformed or the group is empty.

member.name: M:RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.ParseGraphContext(RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.RDFQueryParserContext)

summary.para: Parses the graph specifier of a GRAPH clause — the VarOrIri between the keyword and the group's opening brace — into the that will decorate the scope's patterns as their context.

SPARQL grammar: VarOrIri ::= Var | iri. A variable (?g / $g) becomes an that the engine binds per-quadruple; an IRI (an IRIREF or a prefixed name resolved through the prologue) becomes a fixed . A literal or a blank node in this position is invalid and is rejected with an : the model's pattern context accepts only an RDFContext or an RDFVariable.

member.exception: When the specifier is missing, a literal, or a blank node.

summary.para: Parses a Basic Graph Pattern — an unbraced sequence of triple patterns — and packages it into a fresh . A BGP is the SPARQL analogue of a set of Turtle triples: it uses the same predicate-object list (;) and object list (,) shorthands, and the same a verb for rdf:type.
SPARQL grammar: TriplesBlock ::= TriplesSameSubjectPath ('.' TriplesBlock?)?.

The triple scan terminates at any of the group-body boundaries handled by : a }, a nested {, a graph-pattern keyword, or end of input. The resulting pattern group is returned ready to be appended to the accumulator in .

Collapses a list of algebra members into a single , applying the minimum wrapping needed for the engine to evaluate them as one unit:
Empty list — returns an empty (trivially satisfied, zero rows filtered). This handles the legal SPARQL case of an empty group {}.
Single element — returns the element unchanged. No wrapping overhead.
Multiple elements — wraps them in a SELECT * subquery via so the engine joins them sequentially as a single unit. This is essential when the multi-element list must serve as one operand of a binary algebra operator (e.g. the left side of a MINUS node): without the wrapping, the engine would not know which subset of the query members belongs to the operator's left scope.
Wraps the given list of algebra members into a fresh, wildcard-projection SELECT * subquery so that they are evaluated as a single joined unit by Mirella's query engine.

This wrapping is used exclusively when a group body holding multiple joined members must serve as the single left or right operand of a binary algebra operator (e.g. the left side of a MINUS node, or an operand of UNION). Without the subquery boundary, the engine's CombineTables left-fold would join ALL query members of the outer query indiscriminately rather than respecting the scoping that the braces implied in the original SPARQL text.

Sets the IsOptional flag to true on any type of algebra member, regardless of its concrete run-time type. This is the single place where OPTIONAL semantics are applied to a parsed operand so that Mirella's evaluation engine can distinguish optional from mandatory joins.

The method handles the three concrete member types that can appear as the operand of OPTIONAL:
— the common case: a plain group of triple patterns.
— an inline subquery (multi-element group collapsed to a single subquery by ); its IsOptional property controls whether the engine left-joins or inner-joins it.
— an OPTIONAL whose operand is itself a nested algebra tree (e.g. OPTIONAL { { A } UNION { B } }); the tree node's IsOptional property tells the engine to treat the whole tree as an optional branch.
Attaches a single algebra member to a , routing it to the correct Add… method based on the member's concrete run-time type.

The three member types that the parser can produce are:
— a set of triple patterns; added via .
— an inline subquery (e.g. a multi-member group body collapsed by , or an explicit SubSelect); added via .
— a binary algebra tree node (Union / Minus / Optional-operator); added via .
— a SERVICE (federated query) member; added via .

member.name: M:RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.ParseHavingClause(RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.RDFQueryParserContext,RDFSharp.Query.RDFGroupByModifier)
member.summary: Parses the body of a HAVING clause (the HAVING keyword has already been consumed by ) into a single free boolean expression set on the . Each HavingCondition is a bracketed expression ('(' Expression ')'); multiple space-separated conditions are conjoined (HavingCondition+ is implicitly ANDed). The expression grammar is reused verbatim via , with the context's switched on so that aggregate calls (COUNT(?e), AVG(?g), ...) resolve to references over their aggregator columns — which is what unlocks the full HAVING power (disjunctions, aggregate on the right-hand side, non-comparison constraints, and aggregates not present in the SELECT projection, served by a hidden aggregator).
member.exception: When HAVING appears without a group (no GROUP BY and no projected aggregate), or no condition is found.

member.name: M:RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.ResolveHavingAggregateReference(RDFSharp.Query.RDFGroupByModifier,RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.RDFParsedAggregator,System.Int32@)

Either way an is returned, so the condition reads the column at evaluation time yet re-prints the original aggregate call.

member.name: M:RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.ParseSolutionModifiers(RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.RDFQueryParserContext,System.Action{RDFSharp.Query.RDFModifier},System.Collections.Generic.List{RDFSharp.Query.RDFAggregator})

summary.para: Parses the trailing solution-modifier section of a SELECT query and attaches the resulting modifier objects via . Scanning stops as soon as a token that is not a recognized modifier keyword is encountered; that token is pushed back so the caller can process it (or simply ignore it at end of input).

SPARQL grammar:
SolutionModifier ::= GroupClause? HavingClause? OrderClause? LimitOffsetClauses? LimitOffsetClauses ::= LimitClause OffsetClause? | OffsetClause LimitClause?
All five clauses are handled: GROUP BY and HAVING (delegated to / ) plus ORDER BY, LIMIT and OFFSET. Modifiers are accepted in any order for leniency; if the same modifier appears twice the object-model silently ignores the duplicate.

member.exception: When a recognized modifier keyword is followed by a malformed body.

member.name: M:RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.ParseOrderByModifier(RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.RDFQueryParserContext,System.Action{RDFSharp.Query.RDFModifier})

summary.para:
SPARQL grammar:
OrderClause ::= 'ORDER' 'BY' OrderCondition+ OrderCondition ::= ( ( 'ASC' | 'DESC' ) '(' Expression ')' ) | ( Constraint | Var )
The full grammar is supported: an orders by a single ordering key, an — a bare variable being just its simplest form. So both expression conditions (e.g. ORDER BY STRLEN(?label), ASC(?x + 1)) and bare variables are accepted; a bare condition (variable or expression) implies ASC. At least one order condition is required after BY; anything that is not a recognised condition (e.g. the LIMIT keyword) is pushed back so can process it.

member.exception: When 'BY' is missing or no order condition is found.

member.name: M:RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.ParsePrologue(RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.RDFQueryParserContext)

summary.para: Parses the SPARQL prologue — a (possibly empty) sequence of BASE <iri> and PREFIX label: <iri> declarations — populating the context's resolver as it goes.

Parsing stops at the first token that is neither BASE nor PREFIX (typically the query form keyword SELECT/ASK/CONSTRUCT/DESCRIBE, or an opening brace). That token is left unconsumed in the reader so the caller can dispatch on it.

summary.para: Parses a SubSelect — the nested SELECT query that may stand in for a group graph pattern's body. The 'SELECT' keyword has been confirmed by the caller (via ) but NOT yet consumed; this method consumes it and then delegates the rest of the SELECT surface to , so the subquery gets the full SELECT grammar for free: the DISTINCT/REDUCED modifier, the * / variable / (expr AS ?v) projection, the WHERE clause, and the trailing ORDER BY / LIMIT / OFFSET solution modifiers.

SPARQL grammar: SubSelect ::= SelectClause WhereClause SolutionModifier ValuesClause. A SubSelect carries no prologue of its own (BASE/PREFIX are top-level only), which is exactly why this method does NOT parse a prologue — it enters directly at the SELECT clause. The returned query is flagged as a subquery () when the caller attaches it via , which is what makes the printer omit the prologue for it.

member.exception: When any of the nested SELECT sub-clauses is malformed.

member.name: M:RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.ParseTriplesBlock(RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.RDFQueryParserContext,RDFSharp.Query.RDFPatternGroup)

summary.para: Parses a TriplesBlock — a sequence of triple patterns separated by . — and collects the resulting instances into .
SPARQL grammar: TriplesBlock ::= TriplesSameSubjectPath ('.' TriplesBlock?)?.

Each "triple" in SPARQL can in fact be a full predicate-object list (multiple predicate-object pairs on the same subject, separated by ;) and an object list (multiple objects on the same subject+predicate, separated by ,), exactly as in Turtle.

The scan terminates early (without consuming the terminating character) at any of these block boundaries, leaving the character on the reader for the parent caller to process:
} — the end of the enclosing GroupGraphPattern.
{ — the start of a nested GroupGraphPattern.
A recognized graph-pattern keyword (OPTIONAL, MINUS, UNION, …) — a GraphPatternNotTriples element follows; it is left on the reader for to dispatch on.
End of input (-1) — the underlying reader is exhausted.
A . after the last triple before a block boundary is optional (per the SPARQL grammar) and is consumed silently.

member.param: The pattern group to which parsed triple patterns are added.
member.exception: When a triple inside the block is malformed.

PredicateObjectList ::= Verb ObjectList ( ';' ( Verb ObjectList )? )*

summary.para: Emits a single triple pattern into , applying the active GRAPH context if one is in force. This is the ONE place where the per-pattern context decoration lives, so both ordinary object-list triples and the triples synthesised by blank-node / collection desugaring share identical contextualisation behaviour.

GRAPH contextualisation: when .ActiveContext is non-null (an RDFContext fixed IRI or an RDFVariable), the FOUR-argument constructor is used so the context decorates the triple, and the scope's WasUsed flag is flipped so the GRAPH dispatcher can tell its scope was non-empty (the scope is a value tuple, so flipping WasUsed means re-assigning the slot while keeping the same ActiveContext). Outside any GRAPH clause the THREE-argument constructor is used (default graph). The RDFPattern constructor also enforces SPARQL's term-position rules (e.g. a literal in subject position is rejected), surfaced as RDFQueryException.

list.item: Labelled blank node (_:x) → a fresh-but-stable shared by every occurrence of the same label (see ).
Blank-node property list ([ … ] / []) → desugared by , which emits the nested triples and returns the fresh variable for the blank node.
Collection (( … ) / ()) → desugared by into an rdf:first/rdf:rest/rdf:nil chain; returns the head variable, or rdf:nil for the empty collection.
Concrete term (IRI, prefixed name, literal, numeric/boolean) → delegated to the shared Turtle term-reader via .

A fresh is synthesised for the blank node; when the brackets contain a predicate-object list, those triples are emitted into with that variable as their subject. The variable is returned so the caller can use the blank node as the subject or object of an enclosing triple.
SPARQL grammar: BlankNodePropertyList ::= '[' PropertyListNotEmpty ']', plus the ANON ::= '[' WS* ']' token for the empty form.

member.exception: When the brackets are unbalanced or the inner list is malformed.

member.name: M:RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.ParseCollection(RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.RDFQueryParserContext,RDFSharp.Query.RDFPatternGroup)

summary.para: Parses an RDF collection — ( item1 item2 … ) — and desugars it into the canonical rdf:first/rdf:rest/rdf:nil linked-list triples (SPARQL §17.4 / Turtle collection translation). Each list node is a fresh ; the head variable is returned so the collection can be used as the subject or object of an enclosing triple. The empty collection () desugars to no triples at all and is represented directly by rdf:nil.
SPARQL grammar: Collection ::= '(' GraphNode+ ')'; GraphNode ::= VarOrTerm | TriplesNode, so an item may itself be a variable, a term, a nested collection or a blank-node property list.

SPEC FIDELITY: unlike RDFSharp's Turtle deserialiser, the desugaring deliberately does NOT emit any rdf:type rdf:List typing triple — the SPARQL collection translation is purely rdf:first/rdf:rest/rdf:nil. Adding the typing triple would over-constrain the pattern, making it match only lists explicitly typed as rdf:List in the data.

member.returns: The fresh head variable of the list, or rdf:nil for the empty collection.
member.exception: When the parentheses are unbalanced or an item is malformed.

member.name: M:RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.NewAnonymousBlankNodeVariable(RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.RDFQueryParserContext)
member.summary: Synthesises a fresh for an anonymous blank node (the [] / [ … ] node, or an internal collection list node). The name uses a reserved-looking, valid VARNAME prefix and a monotonic counter so each anonymous node is distinct and round-trips as a plain variable: _BNODE0, _BNODE1, …

summary.para: RDFQueryParserContext bundles the mutable state that belongs to a single SPARQL parse run. It is created fresh for every call to and is never shared across threads or across multiple parse invocations.
The context is sealed because it has no extension points: the only reason to pass it around is to give every parser helper function access to the shared reader position and the resolver.

The Turtle parsing context that the SPARQL parser borrows for all low-level term recognition. It carries two resources:
Reader — the RDFPushbackReader wrapping the SPARQL command text, which the lexer advances one code point at a time and can push characters back onto when needed.
Resolver — the RDFTermResolver wired into , so that every Turtle term-parser (ParseURI, ParseValue, ParseQNameOrBoolean, …) automatically uses the SPARQL prologue's BASE and PREFIX declarations for IRI resolution.

By reusing RDFTurtle's context struct, the SPARQL parser can call all Turtle term-parsers verbatim without any adaptation — the only difference is that the resolver behind the context is an instead of a graph-backed one.

The autonomous resolver that accumulates the BASE and PREFIX declarations of this query's prologue as they are parsed. It is the same resolver instance that is wired into , exposed directly here so that can push new bindings into it via and .

The GRAPH scope currently in force while triple patterns are being built — a single value pairing the two pieces of state that must always live and die together:
ActiveContext — the graph specifier of the innermost enclosing GRAPH clause. It is null whenever no GRAPH clause is active (the default graph), in which case builds plain three-argument patterns; when it is non-null, every triple pattern emitted by ParseObjectList is built with the four-argument constructor so the context decorates the pattern. The value is always one of the two types the model accepts as a pattern context: an (a fixed graph IRI) or an (a dynamic graph variable the engine binds per-quadruple).
WasUsed — whether at least one triple pattern was actually built under the ActiveContext currently in force. ParseObjectList raises it every time it emits a context-decorated pattern. It is the detection mechanism for the forbidden empty GRAPH (GRAPH ?g {} / GRAPH <iri> {}): if a GRAPH scope produces no contextualised pattern, WasUsed is still false on exit and the dispatcher rejects the clause.

This single shared slot is written ONLY by the GRAPH dispatcher () with a strict save → set → recurse → restore discipline. Bundling both fields into ONE value is what makes that discipline atomic: the dispatcher saves and restores a single tuple rather than juggling two variables in lock-step. The discipline gives SPARQL's innermost-shadowing semantics for free — a nested GRAPH overrides the slot for its own sub-scope and restores the outer value on exit, so each triple pattern is contextualised by the GRAPH that most tightly encloses it, and a nested GRAPH never falsely satisfies the emptiness check of its enclosing GRAPH.

Monotonic counter feeding the names of the FRESH variables that the parser synthesises for every ANONYMOUS blank node it desugars — the empty [], each blank-node property list [ … ], and every internal list node of a collection ( … ). Each call to increments it, so two anonymous blank nodes in the same query never collide.

DESIGN NOTE (decided 2026-06-11). In SPARQL a blank node inside a query is an EXISTENTIAL — it behaves like a non-distinguished variable, matching any term in that position. RDFSharp's engine, however, treats a blank-node RDFResource in a pattern as a CONSTANT (only a fixed-position hole that is RDFVariable is a join hole). Desugaring blank nodes into fresh blank-node resources would therefore never match real data. So the parser maps EVERY query blank node — the anonymous ones here and the labelled _:x ones in — onto fresh instances, which the engine evaluates with the intended existential semantics.

Maps each LABELLED blank node label (the x of a _:x token, without the _: prefix) to the single that represents it throughout this query. Looking the label up here guarantees that every occurrence of the same _:x resolves to the SAME variable, exactly as SPARQL requires a repeated blank node label to denote the same node.

Comparison is ordinal because blank node labels are case-sensitive in the SPARQL grammar (even though the resulting RDFVariable name is upper-cased by RDFVariable itself). See the design note on for why labelled blank nodes become variables too.

Diversion target for the triple patterns produced while a TEMPLATE is being parsed — a CONSTRUCT graph template or a SPARQL UPDATE QuadData/QuadPattern. It is null during the normal (WHERE-clause) flow; the relevant template parser sets it to a fresh list for the duration of the { … } template block and resets it to null immediately after.

WHY A SEPARATE SINK. A template is a set of instances attached via (CONSTRUCT) or AddInsert/DeleteTemplate (UPDATE), NOT a pattern group. Crucially it must preserve fully-GROUND triples (e.g. CONSTRUCT { <a> <b> <c> } or INSERT DATA { <a> <b> <c> }) that would silently drop (its guard keeps only patterns that carry at least one variable). Routing the template through this sink lets the whole triple machine (predicate-object/object lists, the a verb, blank nodes and collections) be reused verbatim while the single emission chokepoint diverts every pattern here instead of into a pattern group — bypassing that guard so ground template triples survive.

CONTEXT-AWARE. When a GRAPH scope is active (UPDATE QuadData GRAPH iri { … } blocks), diverts a four-argument (quad) pattern carrying that context; CONSTRUCT templates never open a GRAPH scope, so they always collect plain three-argument triples.

Optional aggregate-aware hook for the expression parser. summary.para: RDFQueryLexer is the lexing layer of the SPARQL parser: the low-level reader primitives (code-point read/peek/unread, keyword runs, variables, terms), the structural-punctuation helpers, and the character-class predicates shared by every file.

It is a standalone static class rather than a partial of so the lexing concern is cleanly separable; the parser files import it via using static RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryLexer; so their existing unqualified calls (SkipWhitespace(…), ReadCodePoint(…), …) keep working. It operates on the parser's (aliased here for brevity), which carries the shared pushback reader and prologue resolver.

member.name: F:RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryLexer.GraphPatternKeywords
member.summary:
The set of SPARQL keywords that can appear at the GraphPatternNotTriples dispatch point (i.e. wherever a new non-triple element can begin inside a GroupGraphPattern).
This set serves two purposes:
It terminates an ongoing TriplesBlock scan — as soon as one of these keywords is spotted, the triple reader stops so the enclosing group-pattern dispatcher can handle the keyword.
It distinguishes a lone keyword (e.g. "UNION") from a prefixed-name local part that happens to start with the same letters (e.g. "union:foo") — the check in uses this set to decide whether the letter run should be treated as a keyword or as the beginning of a QName token.
Comparison is case-insensitive (SPARQL keywords are case-insensitive per the spec).
Every keyword in this set is dispatched to its own parser by : OPTIONAL / UNION / MINUS (algebra-tree nodes), GRAPH and SERVICE (per-pattern / per-group decorations), FILTER / BIND / VALUES (pattern-group members), and SELECT (which opens a SubSelect, '{' SubSelect '}'). The set therefore also marks every point where a TriplesBlock scan must stop and hand control back to that dispatcher.

member.name: M:RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryLexer.SkipWhitespace(RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.RDFQueryParserContext)
member.summary: Skips any run of whitespace and #-style comments, leaving the reader positioned on the next significant character. Returns the code point of that character (without consuming it), or -1 at EOF. Thin pass-through to RDFTurtle so SPARQL and Turtle share identical whitespace/comment handling.

member.name: M:RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryLexer.ReadKeyword(RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.RDFQueryParserContext)
member.summary: Reads a maximal run of ASCII letters starting at the current position and returns it as a string (empty if the current character is not an ASCII letter). The first non-letter character is unread, so the reader is left exactly at the boundary of the run. SPARQL keywords (SELECT, BASE, PREFIX, ASK, ...) are pure ASCII letters, so this is the primitive used to peek/consume them; callers that only wanted to peek can push the run back with .

summary.para: Reads the maximal run of characters that may form a SPARQL BUILT-IN FUNCTION name and returns it verbatim. Unlike — which accumulates ASCII letters only — this also accepts ASCII digits and the underscore, so function names that contain them are tokenised as a single run: MD5, SHA1, SHA256, SHA384, SHA512, ENCODE_FOR_URI.

Callers position the reader on a leading ASCII LETTER first (a SPARQL built-in name never starts with a digit or underscore), then use this to read the rest of the name; the terminating non-name character is pushed back, exactly as does. A prefixed name's label (which may also contain digits/underscores) is read identically and then rewound on the following :, so the general term reader can re-read the whole prefix:local token.

member.summary: Pushes the characters of the given string back onto the reader, preserving their original order, so a subsequent read returns them again. Used to "un-peek" a keyword run that turned out not to be the one we were looking for.

member.exception: When no sigil is present or the variable name is empty.

member.name: M:RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryLexer.PeekGraphPatternKeyword(RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.RDFQueryParserContext)

summary.para: Peeks at the upcoming letter run to determine whether it is a recognized graph-pattern keyword (OPTIONAL, UNION, MINUS, FILTER, GRAPH, SERVICE, BIND, VALUES, SELECT) that stands alone as an operator, rather than the beginning of a QName-like token such as union:SomeClass.

When a recognized keyword is found, the reader is restored to exactly the position it was at before the call (i.e. the keyword is left unconsumed) and the keyword is returned in uppercase. When the letter run is either not a recognized keyword, or IS a recognized keyword but is immediately followed by a QName-continuer character (digit, '_', or '-'), the reader is equally restored and the empty string is returned.

IMPORTANT: This method does NOT skip leading whitespace. Callers are responsible for having positioned the reader on the first significant (non-whitespace) character BEFORE calling this method — typically by calling first. If the reader is sitting on a whitespace character, will return the empty string immediately (since whitespace is not an ASCII letter), and this method will therefore return the empty string too, even if a keyword follows the whitespace.

member.returns: The recognized keyword in uppercase (e.g. "UNION"), or the empty string if the next token is not a standalone graph-pattern keyword.

member.name: M:RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryLexer.ConsumeKeyword(RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.RDFQueryParserContext)
member.summary: Consumes the current graph-pattern keyword token from the reader. Callers MUST have confirmed via that a keyword is present before calling this: the method simply advances past the letter run with no additional checks.

member.name: M:RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryLexer.ReadCodePoint(RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.RDFQueryParserContext)
member.summary: Reads and returns the next Unicode code point from the underlying pushback reader, advancing the reader position by one code point. Returns -1 at end of input. Thin delegation to RDFTurtle.ReadCodePoint so the SPARQL parser shares the identical pull-style I/O contract.

member.name: M:RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryLexer.PeekCodePoint(RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.RDFQueryParserContext)
member.summary: Returns the next Unicode code point from the reader WITHOUT advancing the reader position (i.e. the same code point will be returned by the next call). Returns -1 at end of input. Used to look ahead by a single character without consuming it.

member.name: M:RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryLexer.UnreadCodePoint(RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.RDFQueryParserContext,System.Int32)
member.summary: Pushes a single Unicode code point back onto the reader so that the next call returns it again. Used when a character has been consumed (e.g. to recognise a token boundary) but should be processed by a subsequent parsing step.

member.name: M:RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryLexer.ExpectChar(RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.RDFQueryParserContext,System.Int32,System.String)

summary.para: Skips any leading whitespace and #-style comments, then verifies that the next significant character is and consumes it.

Used for the structural punctuation of the SPARQL grammar: opening/closing braces ({, }), parentheses ((, )), and similar mandatory delimiters. When the expected character is not found, a descriptive is thrown naming the grammar context (e.g. "WHERE clause") so the author knows which construct is malformed.

member.param: The Unicode code point that must be present next.
Human-readable label for the grammar construct (used in error messages).
member.exception: When the next significant character is not .

summary.para: Skips whitespace/comments and, if the next significant character equals , consumes it and returns true. Otherwise leaves the reader positioned on that character (unchanged) and returns false.
Used for optional single-character tokens such as the * wildcard in SELECT projections.

Skips whitespace/comments and, if the upcoming ASCII-letter run equals (case-insensitively), consumes it and returns true. Otherwise restores the reader to exactly the position it was at before the call and returns false.
Used for keywords that are syntactically optional in the SPARQL grammar: WHERE, DISTINCT, REDUCED, and BY (in ORDER BY).

member.name: M:RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryLexer.ParseInteger(RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryParser.RDFQueryParserContext,System.String)

summary.para: Skips whitespace/comments and parses a non-negative decimal integer literal, returning its value as a 32-bit integer. Used for the LIMIT and OFFSET clause values.

member.param: Human-readable label for the containing grammar construct (used in error messages).
member.exception: When no decimal digit is present at the current reader position.

member.name: M:RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryLexer.DescribeCodePoint(System.Int32)
member.summary: Produces a human-readable description of a Unicode code point for use in parse-error messages: returns the character enclosed in single quotes (e.g. '{') or the phrase "end of input" when the code point is -1 (EOF sentinel).

member.name: M:RDFSharp.Query.RDFQueryLexer.IsAsciiLetter(System.Int32)
member.summary: Returns true when is an ASCII letter (A–Z or a–z). Used by to accumulate the maximal letter run that may be a keyword.

summary.para: Returns true when is a valid FIRST character of a SPARQL variable name (VARNAME).

SPARQL grammar: VARNAME ::= ( PN_CHARS_U | [0-9] ) ( PN_CHARS_U | [0-9] | … )*. The first character must be a PN_CHARS_U character (letter, underscore, or non-ASCII Unicode letter/digit in the PN_CHARS_U set) or an ASCII decimal digit.
Returns true when is a valid CONTINUATION character inside a SPARQL variable name (VARNAME) — i.e. any character valid at position 2 or later.

SPARQL grammar: the tail of a VARNAME may contain PN_CHARS_U, decimal digits, and additional Unicode ranges: U+00B7 (middle dot), U+0300–U+036F (combining diacritics), and U+203F–U+2040 (undertie / character tie). The hyphen - is intentionally excluded: unlike Turtle's PN_CHARS, SPARQL VARNAME does not allow hyphens after the first character.

member.summary: Absolute base IRI declared by a SPARQL BASE directive, used to resolve relative IRIs. Remains the empty string until a BASE directive is parsed (SPARQL allows queries with no base).

member.name: F:RDFSharp.Query.RDFSPARQLTermResolver.prefixLabelToNamespaceUri
member.summary: Prefix-label => namespace-URI bindings declared by the SPARQL PREFIX directives. The empty string key represents the default namespace declared as PREFIX : <...>. Comparison is ordinal because prefix labels are case-sensitive in SPARQL.

member.name: P:RDFSharp.Query.RDFSPARQLTermResolver.BaseUri
member.summary: Base IRI against which the Turtle term-parsers resolve relative IRI references. Mirrors the value last supplied through a SPARQL BASE directive (empty when none was given).

member.name: P:RDFSharp.Query.RDFSPARQLTermResolver.DeclaredPrefixes
member.summary: The prefix-label => namespace-URI bindings explicitly declared by this query's PREFIX directives, in declaration order. The SPARQL parser reads these back to re-attach them to the parsed query (via RDFSelectQuery.AddPrefix), so that the resulting query re-serializes its prologue identically. The leniency fallbacks (well-known register prefixes) are deliberately NOT included here: only the prefixes the query author actually wrote belong in its prologue.

member.name: M:RDFSharp.Query.RDFSPARQLTermResolver.SetBaseIri(System.String)
member.summary: Records the absolute base IRI carried by a SPARQL BASE <absoluteBaseIri> directive. A later BASE directive overrides an earlier one, matching SPARQL's "last declaration wins" semantics.

member.name: M:RDFSharp.Query.RDFSPARQLTermResolver.RegisterPrefix(System.String,System.String)
member.summary: Records a prefix-to-namespace binding carried by a SPARQL PREFIX label: <namespaceUri> directive. A null/empty label is the default namespace. A later declaration of the same label overrides the earlier one, matching SPARQL's "last declaration wins" semantics.

member.name: M:RDFSharp.Query.RDFSPARQLTermResolver.ResolveNamespace(System.String)
member.summary:
Resolves a prefix label to its namespace URI for the Turtle term-parsers. Resolution order:
a namespace explicitly declared by a PREFIX directive of this very query (always wins);
RATIFIED LENIENCY: for a non-empty label that was never declared, fall back to the well-known prefixes of the global RDFNamespaceRegister (rdf, rdfs, xsd, owl, ...) so that common vocabularies can be used without an explicit PREFIX declaration.
Returns null when the label cannot be resolved (e.g. the default namespace was never declared, or an unknown prefix is used): the caller surfaces this as a parse error.
